newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cathay Pacific 1996 profit surges.
newsitem.headline: Cathay Pacific 1996 profit surges.

text.p: Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd reported a 27.9 percent surge in 1996 net profit on Wednesday, meeting market expectations as the Hong Kong flag carrier battled to keep costs under control.
The company posted net profit of HK$3.81 billion (US$488 million), boosted by an exceptional gain of HK$541.0 million from selling down its stake in Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd.
Turnover rose to HK$32.38 billion from HK$30.45 billion.
"We are pleased with 1996. It was a very creditable performance," said chairman Peter Sutch on Wednesday.
The net profit figure was within market expectations.
Analysts had predicted net profit of HK$3.7-HK$4.0 billion and praised the company for its ability to keep costs under control.

"They have done quite well. The results are broadly in line with our expectations," said Merrill Lynch analyst Wendy Wong. "On the cost side they have actually done better. They are obviously cutting costs quite aggressively."
Cathay Pacific said its total airline operating costs rose 6.5 percent to HK$26.67 billion. It said increasing cost pressures and lower yields had required constant attention.
Cathay Pacific's cargo business posted turnover growth of 5.6 percent to HK$6.11 billion, representing about 20.5 percent of Cathay's total traffic turnover.
It said its cargo division carried 568,000 tonnes of cargo in 1996, up 7.0 percent from the previous year.
Cathay Pacific said it planned total capital expenditure of nearly HK$20 billion for the coming two to three years.

The airline would spend roughly half of that sum, US$450 million, on its headquarters at Hong Kong's new international airport at Chep Lap Kok which is scheduled to open in April 1988, said managing director David Turnbull.
"We (also) shall be taking delivery of aircraft up to the middle of 1999 at a value of around HK$10 billion," he said.
The chairman said he was optimistic about the airline's future prospects.
"We face the future from a position of considerable strength," Sutch said. "If we can hold yields where they are that will give us very satisfactory results."

While the industry was no longer gaining significant cost efficiencies from technological improvements, the airline would reap cost efficiencies from its new, much younger fleet of aircraft, said Sutch.
"I believe we have the resources to ensure Cathay Pacific enters the new century as a world-class, customer-driven airline producing superior financial returns," he added.
